Chapter 17

The lesson: the same engine, out of $derived

Nine cells whose values are $deriveds that read each other through a lookup function and nothing else. No edges recorded, no order computed — and it agrees with the hand-written engine on every edit, count for count, because it is the same algorithm. Until a cycle, where it needs a graph of its own.

By the end of this chapter

See that Svelte’s runtime is a spreadsheet engine with the cells hidden, and know the two things a runtime cannot give a spreadsheet.

The header is the argument of the whole course in a comment. Read it, then read the class, and notice that there is no code anywhere that says “A3 depends on A1”. The one place that reads a formula’s references, further down, does it only to find cycles, and the blocks after the class say why it must.

value is a $derived.by as a class field. It reads this.input and, through the sheet, whichever other cells the formula references — and those reads are the dependencies. Svelte records them as the derived runs. Change A1 and every derived that read A1, transitively, is marked and recomputed in dependency order, once each. That is steps one to three of chapter 09 with no code for any of them.

onCycle is derived too, and it is made in the constructor rather than beside its siblings. A $derived can be the first assignment to a field inside the constructor, exactly as $state can, and here that is the honest place: the expression reads this.name and this.#sheet, which only exist once the constructor has set them. (The derived would not run before then anyway — deriveds are lazy — but TypeScript, reading a field initialiser, cannot know that, and says so.)

evaluations += 1 inside a derived is a side effect, and the comment admits it: counting is the lesson. It is counted the way the engine counts — after the cycle check and after the literal check — because the engine evaluates formulas, not cells: a typed number is read, not evaluated, and a cell on a cycle is marked, not evaluated. Count anything else on one side and the two numbers the page puts side by side are measuring different things.

The sheet is nine cells in a plain Map — the map never changes; the cells inside it are what is reactive — and set is one assignment. There is nothing else for it to do, because nothing about a cycle is kept by hand.

Why a cell works out whether it is on a cycle before it reads another cell

Type =C3 into A1 and C3, which averages A1, now feeds A1: a derived that reads itself. Svelte has no answer to that but an exception. In development it notices and throws derived_references_self; that check sits behind if (DEV) in the runtime, so a production build has none, and the deriveds call each other until the stack runs out. The first version of this file caught the overflow in the formula’s catch and showed #ERROR! — after hundreds of evaluations for one edit — and the page never recovered. So a cell asks first, from the formulas alone, whether following its references leads back to it, and a cell that does answers #CYCLE! without reading another cell. reachesItself reads inputs and never values, so it cannot be caught in the cycle it is looking for. That is a graph again — the engine’s, for nine cells — which is the lesson: a cycle is a value only because somebody kept one.

Why each cell derives its own answer, and not one set for the sheet

The second version kept a $state flag on every cell and had set write all nine after each edit. It worked, but a value that is a pure function of other state was being copied by hand, and only set kept it right: write cell.input directly and the flags went stale, and the crash came back. The obvious repair is one $derived set of cyclic cells for the whole sheet, with each cell’s flag derived from it. That is correct, and it costs. Every cell then depends on every input, so every edit asks all nine cells whether they are still right — and Svelte moves a derived’s version forward only when its value changes, so a cell whose last re-run came out the same, like A3’s "A1", looks older than the cells it reads and is worked out again for nothing. Measured: once A1 had changed, changing B2 evaluated five formulas where the engine evaluated four, and the fifth was A3, which reads neither. Deriving the answer per cell, from the inputs that cell can reach, gives each flag exactly the dependencies its value already has. An edit wakes the same cells it would have woken anyway, and across eighteen thousand random edits — half of them direct writes to input — the two sides never disagreed on a value and the deriveds never did more work than the engine.

The page

Both sheets start from the same nine formulas. edit writes the same input into both and records how many formulas each evaluated — the engine reports it in its Recalc; the reactive side is read in full so the deriveds run now, and the difference in the counter is the answer. The engine is not reactive, so engineInput and engineValue read engineVersion before they read the engine: the one number edit bumps is what makes the template ask again, the same contract the grid has with the sheet.

Three declaration tags open each engine cell, and only the third is a $derived. The name and its address are fixed for as long as the item exists — the each is keyed by the column letter — so they are plain tags, worked out once when the item is made. The value is not fixed: engineValue reads engineVersion, which every edit changes while the item lives, so {const value = $derived(…)} is what keeps the number and its error colouring following the engine. Written as a plain tag it would be worked out once, and the left-hand sheet would never change.

The reactive side needs no $derived in its markup at all. {const name = …} and {const cell = …} are plain for the same reason as the engine’s name and address, and the cell’s value is already a $derived inside the class, so reading cell.value in the markup is enough to follow it. Chapter 19 has the rule that decides between the two kinds of tag.

Why no reactive cell is wrapped in a boundary

The first version put a <svelte:boundary> round each reactive output, with a failed snippet that said cycle!. Driving the page in a real browser showed that snippet never ran: the formula’s catch got to the exception first. With the catch taken out so the exception could reach it, the whole page became the error page instead. Svelte hands an exception thrown inside a $derived to the boundary of the effect that created the derived, and these deriveds were created by the page’s script — so the page’s boundary, the root +error.svelte, is the one that heard about it. A boundary catches what its own content throws while it renders; a value computed somewhere else fails where it was made. With cycles found before any cell is read, nothing here throws, and the comment in the markup says why there is no boundary. The engine still has two things the runtime cannot give a spreadsheet: cycles as values for a million cells, and a million cells that are not each a signal, which is chapter 15’s line. Neither makes it a different algorithm.

Where the two counts part, and why that is Svelte doing less

Type 5.0 into A2 while it holds 5. The engine evaluates the five formulas downstream of an edited cell, because its dirty set is worked out before anything is evaluated. The deriveds evaluate none: A2’s derived runs, produces the same number, and Svelte compares each new value with the old one — a derived whose value is unchanged notifies nobody. The engine could do the same, by stopping the wave at a cell whose value came out equal. It does not, because it finds cycles as whatever is left of the dirty set when the sort runs out, and that only works if the whole dirty set is evaluated. It is the one place the two part ways on a sheet with no cycle, and the page says so rather than claiming a perfect match.

The first end-to-end test edits one side, then the other, and asserts all eighteen outputs agree — and that both hints name the same count: seven formulas for A1, four for B2. It is the test that says the two are the same thing. The second makes the cycle the page tells you to make, checks both sides call it #CYCLE! in the same cells and both evaluated two formulas, and breaks it again: every value must come back. The third pins down the one difference, so that a change to either side that made it disappear — or grow — would be noticed.

Checkpoint

  • You can say where the dependency edges are in ReactiveCell and why there is no code for them.
  • You can say what Svelte does with a derived that reads itself, in development and in a production build, and why each reactive cell looks at references before it reads another cell.
  • You can explain why one derived set of cyclic cells for the whole sheet makes the counts disagree, and per-cell derivation does not.
  • You can say which boundary hears about an exception thrown inside a $derived.
  • You can name the two reasons the hand-written engine exists even though $derived does the same thing.
